outcomes.text: Explain how a finite list and a recursive rule can describe an unbounded set.
Apply a rule twice and explain how it groups its inputs or rejects an unfinished one.
Explain how grammar rules license sentences and describe their structure.

opening.prompt: If the complete list contains “Iris rests” and “Leo waits”, does “Iris rests and Leo waits” belong to it?

options.text: Yes, because both parts are listed.
options.feedback: The list contains the individual parts. It needs an added rule to permit their combination.

options.text: No, because the combined sentence is absent.
options.feedback: A complete list contains every member of that fixed set.

options.text: Only if Iris comes first.
options.feedback: The list supplies no combination in either order.

opening.prompt: If “and” joins two complete sentences, which input is unfinished?

options.text: Iris rests and
options.feedback: There is no sentence after “and”.

options.text: Mina waves
options.feedback: This input is a complete sentence.

options.text: Leo waits
options.feedback: This input has a subject and predicate.

opening.prompt: What can the output of the toy sentence-combination rule become?

options.text: A new rule
options.feedback: The rule stays the same.

options.text: A single word
options.feedback: The result is a complete sentence.

options.text: An input to the same rule
options.feedback: The rule produces an S, and it accepts S as an input.

opening.prompt: In “[Iris rests and Leo waits] and [Mina waves]”, what is the first input to the last step?

options.text: Iris rests
options.feedback: This was a starting sentence, but the first bracket includes the earlier combination.

options.text: Iris rests and Leo waits
options.feedback: The entire first bracket serves as one input.

options.text: Mina waves
options.feedback: This is the second input.

opening.prompt: What does a labelled tree describe about a sequence?

options.text: How its words are grouped
options.feedback: The branches show the parts and their relationships.

options.text: How often the sequence is used
options.feedback: The tree gives structure, while frequency needs different evidence.

options.text: Who first said it
options.feedback: The labels describe grammatical categories.

closing.prompt: A toy grammar lists “Ren reads” and “Ivo sings” and permits S → S and S. How can it derive “Ren reads and Ivo sings and Ren reads”?

options.text: Write a new rule for three sentences.
options.feedback: Two applications of the original rule suffice.

options.text: Apply the rule once with three inputs.
options.feedback: Each application takes two inputs.

options.text: Join the two base sentences, then join the result with another base sentence.
options.feedback: The first result is an S, so it qualifies as an input to the second step.

closing.prompt: Why does the toy grammar fail to derive “Ivo sings and”?

options.text: It uses a verb.
options.feedback: “Ivo sings” is already a complete base sentence.

options.text: It lacks a complete second sentence.
options.feedback: The rule requires an S on each side of “and”.

options.text: It repeats a base sentence.
options.feedback: The sequence contains only one complete base sentence.

closing.prompt: Which grouping records a final step with “Ren reads” as the first input and “Ivo sings and Nia listens” as the second?

options.text: [Ren reads] and [Ivo sings and Nia listens]
options.feedback: The second bracket preserves the earlier combination.

options.text: [Ren reads and Ivo sings] and [Nia listens]
options.feedback: This version groups a different pair first.

options.text: [Ren reads] and [Ivo sings] and [Nia listens]
options.feedback: This version does not show which pair formed the earlier result.

closing.prompt: The toy grammar uses S → NP VP and licenses “The bird sings”. Why does this rule fail for “Sings the bird”?

options.text: The sequence has no noun phrase.
options.feedback: “The bird” is an NP. Check its position.

options.text: The sequence has no verb phrase.
options.feedback: “Sings” is a VP in this toy grammar. Check its position.

options.text: The VP comes before the NP.
options.feedback: The rule specifies the order as well as the categories.

closing.prompt: What does a grammar supply for a licensed sentence in addition to a membership decision?

options.text: A count of how often it has been said.
options.feedback: Frequency is separate from the structure assigned by the grammar.

options.text: A structural description.
options.feedback: The rules specify the permitted combinations and their grouping.

options.text: A list of every future use.
options.feedback: A grammar describes a pattern that can apply to novel sentences.
